title: React Security Core Check
description: Check your understanding of React security risks, XSS, CSRF, authentication storage, dependencies, secure rendering, and environment mistakes.
author: DailyCoder

questions.prompt: Which statement about frontend authorization is correct?

options.text: Frontend checks improve UX but server-side authorization must enforce access
Hiding a button fully protects an API

questions.explanation: The frontend can guide users, but the server must enforce sensitive authorization rules.

questions.prompt: How does React help reduce basic text injection XSS risk?

options.text: It escapes values rendered as text by default
It blocks every script URL automatically

questions.explanation: React escapes text interpolation by default, which helps prevent many basic XSS cases.

options.text: It can render untrusted HTML as executable markup if not sanitized

questions.explanation: Rendering raw HTML requires strong trust and sanitization because it bypasses React text escaping.

options.text: A browser sending authenticated cookie-based requests triggered by another site

questions.explanation: CSRF is relevant when credentials such as cookies are automatically attached to cross-site requests.

questions.prompt: Which cookie setting helps reduce CSRF risk?
questions.explanation: SameSite controls when cookies are sent in cross-site contexts.

questions.prompt: Which are safer practices for authentication in a React app? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Use secure, HttpOnly cookies when appropriate for sessions
Treat localStorage tokens as exposed to XSS risk
Keep authorization enforcement on the server
Store refresh tokens in a public JavaScript variable

questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies can reduce token exposure, localStorage has XSS risk, and servers must enforce authorization.

options.text: They make dependency resolution more reproducible

questions.explanation: Lockfiles help teams and CI install predictable dependency versions.

questions.prompt: Frontend environment variables bundled into client JavaScript should be treated as public values.
questions.explanation: Anything in the shipped browser bundle can be inspected by users.
